entries.note: Neither deep instability nor dependence on vibes has a shared evidentiary threshold.

entries.test: AI-sector valuations relative to underlying earnings and investment returns, together with evidence of dependence on NVIDIA, would test the bubble and concentration claims.
entries.note: The surrounding argument identifies NVIDIA as the central point of failure.

entries.test: Public demonstrations and independent evaluations of agents reliably completing their advertised autonomous tasks would contradict the claim.
entries.note: The categorical never claim is stronger than a complaint about current reliability.

entries.test: A broad collapse in generative AI investment, valuations and operating businesses would test the predicted collapse.
entries.note: The record includes an asserted eventual collapse, not just a present assessment.

entries.test: NVIDIA's quarterly GPU sales and market valuation would show whether maintaining its value requires uninterrupted sequential GPU sales growth.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies the valuation context.

entries.test: Market weights and the remaining Magnificent 7 stocks' response to a NVIDIA growth setback would test the claim.
entries.note: The record combines a present concentration estimate with a conditional market prediction.

entries.test: Public financial reporting showing profits from generative AI would contradict the factual premise.
entries.note: The passage explicitly makes lack of profits the reason there is no substantive AI trade.

entries.test: Public financial evidence of any company other than NVIDIA earning profits from generative AI at publication would contradict the claim.
The five companies' 2024–2025 AI capital expenditures and AI revenues, alongside fulfillment of their spending commitments, would settle the claim.
entries.note: The stated deadline has passed.

entries.test: Microsoft's AI revenue breakdown, OpenAI contract margins and 2025 capital spending would test the stated figures.
entries.note: “Real” revenue means revenue excluding OpenAI here; it is not an accounting category.
The growth prediction is explicitly qualified by “likely.”

entries.test: Meta's generative AI revenues and attributable operating and investment costs would show whether it was burning cash.
entries.note: “I believe” introduces an asserted financial assessment.
He says the investment will “probably” happen.

entries.test: Representative user surveys and population estimates linking negative AI attitudes to Apple Intelligence's performance would test the claimed effect on millions.
entries.note: The numerical scale gives the assertion factual content despite its inflammatory wording.

entries.test: Public market and spending data would test how strongly changes in the five companies' NVIDIA purchases explain broad US equity-market instability.
entries.note: He disclaims predicting the companies' demise.

entries.test: A significant change in a named buyer's NVIDIA investment and its subsequent attributable effect on broad stock indexes would test the prediction.
entries.note: The wording says changes, although the surrounding argument mainly concerns reductions.

entries.test: Hyperscaler financial disclosures and credible segment estimates would show AI services' losses, revenue and contribution to company revenue growth.
Hyperscalers' reported AI revenues and individual data-center capital expenditure budgets would test the financial assertions.
entries.note: “For no real reason” is an evaluative addition to concrete spending claims.

entries.test: Inflation-adjusted historical AWS buildout expenditures compared with Amazon's 2024 and 2025 capital expenditures would test the comparison.
entries.note: The source compares against Amazon's capital expenditures, not a separately established AI-only total.
Whether an analogy is appropriate is an evaluative judgment as phrased.
“Feels more like” becomes a categorical classification. The feature-versus-infrastructure distinction has no agreed test here.

entries.test: Contemporaneous financial disclosures or credible financial reporting for LLM companies other than Midjourney would test their profitability.
entries.note: Uncertainty about the expressly excluded company does not hedge the claim about the others.
“Do not seem” presents a tentative assessment rather than a firm popularity claim.

entries.test: Cursor's historical prices, model costs, customer growth and June 2025 service changes would test whether loss-making terms drove growth and required replacement.
Cursor's contemporaneous revenues, expenses and losses would settle the concrete profitability assertion.
entries.note: The broader “sign of things to come” has no specified outcome or horizon.

entries.test: Public customer contracts, pricing changes and financial reporting would test whether imposed infrastructure charges increased revenue and covered rising model costs.
entries.note: The assertion describes a financial mechanism, not merely a revenue level.
The revenue prediction is explicitly “highly unlikely.”
“Unlikely to help” is broader than unlikely to achieve profitability. The forecast is explicitly probabilistic.

entries.test: Documented future rate limits or service throttling imposed by OpenAI and Anthropic on high-demand customers would test the prediction.
Public evidence of substantial profitable generative AI businesses outside software subscriptions would contradict the exclusivity claim.
entries.note: The following sentence emphasizes enterprise seat sales.
The normalization drops “suggest.” Justifying a valuation also depends on unspecified growth and discount assumptions.

entries.test: Future contract and pricing changes imposing higher charges or service restrictions on successful customers would test the predicted conduct.
entries.note: “Loot” is rhetorical, but the surrounding pricing discussion supplies concrete predicted behavior.

entries.test: Cursor's revenue milestones, former product terms and costs of serving that product would test whether its $500 million run rate depended on an unaffordable offering.
entries.note: The inference about all coding startups is substantially broader than the Cursor evidence.

entries.test: Perplexity's unit economics, operating expenses and documented business plans would test whether it had a financially viable route to profitability.
entries.note: “Nothing new” is an additional comparative judgment about its search product.
The claim is tentative: “doesn't seem.” The ChatGPT exception appears immediately afterward.

entries.test: Generative AI software companies' profits and revenue growth trajectories compared with earlier major software companies would test the assertion.

entries.note: The text supplies no shared standard for uniqueness or how difficult achieving it must be.
The normalization firms up a thesis that “suggests” exhaustion. “Out of ideas” has no shared operational meaning.

entries.test: Subsequent unilateral pricing changes or access withdrawals by OpenAI and Anthropic would test the predicted recurrence.
entries.note: The preceding paragraph establishes what “do it again” refers to.

entries.test: Generative AI companies' revenues and operating costs would test whether their products earn enough to cover running costs.
entries.note: The surrounding examples give “make sense” a financial reading.
The superlative is a rhetorical denunciation rather than a specified fraud allegation.

entries.test: Agentforce documentation and independent task evaluations would show whether its products can act autonomously beyond chatbot interactions and API retrieval.
entries.note: The surrounding passage defines autonomy as performing tasks without oversight.
The operating-cost component is explicitly “likely”; the performance component is separately testable.
The universal assertion concerns companies' private intent to deceive.

entries.test: Independent evaluations of unchecked coding-agent runs could measure introduced defects and the additional human work required.
entries.note: The intelligence insult accompanies a concrete operational claim.
“These products” becomes all current products, and “likely means” becomes a frequency claim. The terminology assertion remains probabilistic in the source.

entries.test: OpenAI's and Anthropic's annual net losses and historical startup financial records would test the financial comparison.
entries.note: The source says their broader stories are unprecedented, not that billion-dollar annual losses are unprecedented.

entries.test: SoftBank's financing obligations, liquidity, borrowing and credit-rating assessments connected to the OpenAI round would test the claimed financial danger.
entries.note: The following sentences identify concrete debt and credit risks.

entries.test: Public reporting on OpenAI's Stargate commitment, available cash and committed financing sources would test its dependence on SoftBank's funds.
entries.note: This is a present financing-availability claim.

entries.test: OpenAI's and Anthropic's financial projections, cash flows and external funding requirements would test their profitability prospects and funding dependence.
entries.note: The normalization omits the stated requirement for continued infrastructure expansion.

entries.test: Anthropic's unit economics, expenses and financial projections would test whether it had a viable path to profitability.
entries.note: “Desperate” is an evaluative characterization alongside a financial assertion.

entries.test: Comparable-period generative AI revenue estimates for OpenAI, Anthropic and the rest of the industry including hyperscalers would test the claimed majority share.
entries.note: Calling the figure an estimate does not make it an assertion of probability.

entries.test: OpenAI's legal structure at year-end 2025 and its resulting funding and operating viability would test the conditional prediction.
entries.note: If the antecedent did not occur, the conditional was not exercised.

entries.test: OpenAI's cash losses and survival after any cessation of continuing external funding would test the prediction.
entries.note: No deadline is given for funding cessation or failure.

entries.test: Publicly documented unit economics, operating costs and credible financial projections would test whether OpenAI had a viable route to profitability.
Representative adoption surveys, active-user data and paid enterprise deployment records would test the claimed absence of significant generative AI adoption.
entries.note: The surrounding text distinguishes sustained work use from casual experimentation.
The main assessment is that the business is horrifying or terrible.
The profitability premise is factual, but the conclusion defines unprofitable firms as not real businesses.
The claim assigns a private manipulative motive to every such story. The denial of replacement capability is supported by the surrounding text.
The scaling prediction is explicitly attributed to Meta's chief AI scientist. The normalization absorbs that attribution into Zitron's own claim and asserts a marketing motive.
Consciousness has no agreed public evidentiary test; autonomy can be evaluated separately.

entries.test: Industry revenue estimates and contemporaneous media representations of generative AI's revenue scale would test the asserted $50 billion versus $1 trillion discrepancy.
entries.note: “Masquerading” is rhetorical, but the revenue estimate is concrete.
Price movements become pricing levels in the normalization. The proposed alternative market trajectory is counterfactual.
“Terrible” and “worse” are judgments of business quality without a specified ranking criterion.
The claim makes model similarity a cause of difficulty innovating, but supplies no shared standard for innovation or difficulty.

entries.test: A reduction in Microsoft's OpenAI-related infrastructure expansion followed by attributable changes in NVIDIA revenue would test the proposed consequence.
entries.note: The normalization narrows “any changes” to reductions, although reductions are the example given.

entries.test: The six named companies' AI revenues and attributable costs would show whether their AI activities generated billion-dollar losses.
Public revenue attribution, measured customer returns and product-level profit data would test the claimed absence of significant gains and prevalence of losses.
Independent evaluations against advertised capabilities and documented deployments producing financial returns or labor automation would test the claim.

entries.note: “Seems” and uncertainty about survival make the central profitability and viability assessment tentative.

entries.test: A Magnificent 7 company's growth slowdown followed by cuts to loss-making generative AI spending would test the predicted sequence.
entries.note: He predicts that the slowdown itself will occur, rather than merely assuming it.

entries.test: Comparable cost measurements for running larger and reasoning-heavy models would test the asserted model-cost relationship.
entries.note: He expressly allows that inference costs might be falling. The normalization adds a categorical conclusion he does not make.

entries.test: Public evidence that OpenAI and Broadcom produced their custom AI ASIC during 2026 would contradict the prediction.
entries.note: The deadline is the end of 2026, not the evaluation date.

entries.test: Successful substitution of custom ASICs for NVIDIA GPUs and subsequent effects on NVIDIA sales and AI-related equities would test the predicted damage.
AI GPU deployments' attributable revenues, operating costs and investment returns would test whether they lose owners money from installation.
A broad collapse in AI-related valuations and investment would test the predicted bursting of the AI bubble.
entries.note: “Once” treats the collapse as expected, not merely possible.

entries.test: The emergence of autonomous agents demonstrably replacing white-collar workers at the described scale would contradict the never-exist prediction.
entries.note: The replacement prediction is attributed to Amodei; the categorical denial is Zitron's own.

entries.test: Historical market concentration and sensitivity data, alongside the buyers' GPU investment returns, would test the claimed exceptional financial fragility.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies a concrete concentration-and-dependence reading of brittleness.
Confident errors are observable, but “no concept of right or wrong” has no shared operational test or causal criterion here.
He explicitly allows sales, customer expectations or sentiment to constitute slowing momentum, without a shared threshold.
“Could” states a possibility, not a firm collapse prediction under the condition.

entries.test: Public retirement-portfolio data showing widespread severe losses attributable to an AI-market collapse would test the prediction.
Public evidence connecting layoffs to AI infrastructure spending and subsequent financial or productive returns from that infrastructure would test both assertions.
entries.note: The layoff assertion concerns the past; the no-value assertion also commits to future outcomes.

entries.test: Market losses, economic damage and technology-sector contraction attributable to the AI boom would test the forecast.
entries.note: This extracts the factual prediction from a passage that also demands accountability.
This is a demand for accountability, not a prediction that accountability will occur.
